sweep_summary: Both bibliography items are one work — Gralow 1985 'Coreguaje: Tone, Stress, and Intonation' (Brend ed., From Phonology to Discourse, SIL LDAM 9, pp. 3-11), which Glottolog lists twice (141826, 116538). The full article is open on archive.org (Rosetta Project scan, rosettaproject_coe_phon-2; saved to and was read in full: stress is 'basically predictable, though tone was not' (p. 4), 'The first syllable of a stem of a word is usually stressed. Stress is characterized by perceived loudness and length' (p. 4 §1) — verbatim the catalog's deciding quote, so the catalog's fixed-strict initial coding is CONFIRMED with its locator (Gralow 1985:4) correct. Refinements from the same source: two lexical tones (H/L) on disyllabic stems; three stem-derived bisyllabic suffixes (-k'ai, -hai, -koso) also bear stress on their first syllable (p. 8), so words can carry more than one stress; in isolation 'phrase stress' neutralizes the tone contrasts of CVCV nouns (p. 3); the pause-group nucleus is the stressed syllable of the last word (pp. 8-9). Glottolog's URL for 116538 (sil.org/acpub/repository/) is dead and SIL archive entry 18622 is now a Gurindji reader, not Gralow — the Glottolog link should be replaced by the archive.org copy. Best additional first-hand statement (already held by the project from the 9/13 morphstress download, copied into our files): Cook & Criswell 1993, El idioma koreguaje, pp. 10-11: 'El ACENTO no es fonemático. La sílaba inicial de un radical siempre va acentuada, pero puede darse más de una sílaba acentuada por palabra' — always root-initial, non-phonemic, possibly multiple stresses per word; confirms and sharpens ('siempre' vs 'usually') without superseding Gralow 1985 as the primary analysis (Cook & Criswell cite Gralow for the suprasegmentals). Vega Rodríguez 2019 (M2, held by the project) reports the same secondhand ('un accent qui n'est pas phonologique et frappe toujours la première syllabe', citing Cook & Criswell 1993:10-11) and adds that Cristancho Botia & García Moreno 1982 treated Korebaju as a stress language with primary and secondary stress (not obtained; low priority — pre-dates the tone analysis). Not obtained: the full Young, Cook & Gralow 1984 'Fonología del coreguaje' (Sistemas fonológicos 5, SIL, could not be reached by automated download; Gralow note 4 says it contains the suprasegmentals only in outline form) — low priority. all lookups were done by direct download. Nothing read contradicts the catalog.

new_statements.quote: El idioma koreguaje manifiesta dos TONOS distintivos: alto [...] y bajo [...]. En los radicales bisilábicos, las cuatro combinaciones posibles contrastan entre sí, siempre que el radical inicie un sintagma y no sea su núcleo. Si es el núcleo, en cambio, la acentuación a nivel de sintagma las neutraliza completamente, por lo menos en los sintagmas nominales (Gralow, 1985). [...] El ACENTO no es fonemático. La sílaba inicial de un radical siempre va acentuada, pero puede darse más de una sílaba acentuada por palabra. (Para los vestigios de un antiguo sistema de acentuación, véase la sección 1.4.1).
new_statements.translation: The Koreguaje language shows two distinctive TONES: high [...] and low [...]. In disyllabic roots the four possible combinations contrast with one another, provided the root begins a phrase and is not its nucleus. If it is the nucleus, phrase-level stress neutralizes them completely, at least in noun phrases (Gralow 1985). [...] STRESS is not phonemic. The initial syllable of a root is always stressed, but there may be more than one stressed syllable per word. (For the vestiges of an older stress system, see section 1.4.1.)

new_statements.reading: First-hand SIL grammar (the fullest description of the language) stating categorically that stress is non-phonemic and always falls on the root-initial syllable — stronger than Gralow's 'usually' — while adding that a word may carry more than one stressed syllable (the stem-derived bisyllabic suffixes -k'ai/-hai/-koso that Gralow p. 8 says are stressed on their first syllable). Domain is the ROOT/STEM, not the phonological word: a word = stem + suffix cluster has its stress on the stem's first syllable, which is word-initial since Koreguaje is suffixing. This confirms the catalog's fixed: initial syllable coding (initial stress) and Gordon's 'Initial (root)' annotation; the 'more than one stressed syllable' clause and the phrase-level stress that neutralizes tone are refinements, not contradictions. §1.4.1 (pp. 11-12) adds that alternating (stem-then-every-other-syllable) stress is only a reconstructed OLD system, evidenced by suffix allomorphy, not the synchronic pattern.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Agree: fixed-strict initial (root/stem domain) stands. One correction to the compiler reasoning only: Koreguaje is not purely suffixing — Cook & Criswell 1993 §3.1.6 (the scanned textPDF p. 79-80 = printed pp. 73-74) lists two verbal prefixes, ape- 'apenas empezando a' and derivational ka- (e.g. ape-je?e-mo, ka-ku?a-mi). new_statements.quote: In the process of the analysis it finally became evident that stress was basically predictable, though tone was not. [p. 4] ... The first syllable of a stem of a word is usually stressed. Stress is characterized by perceived loudness and length. High pitches tend to be higher toward the beginning of the word, phrase, or sentence than they are toward the end. [p. 4, §1] ... Two-syllable suffixes which have inherent high tone tend to act differently from suffixes without inherent high tone. They also seem to have stress on the first syllable as do stems. Historically these high tone suffixes were probably verb stems [...] These suffixes are: -k'ai benefactive, -hai accompanying movement, -koso probability [p. 8]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Coreguaje has two lexical tones (high, low) plus predictable stress: stress falls on the first syllable of the stem, which is word-initial in this suffixing language; it is realized as loudness and length, and word tone is separate and contrastive. Bisyllabic suffixes with inherent high tone (-k'ai, -hai, -koso; historically verb stems) carry their own stress on their first syllable. In isolation, phrase stress neutralizes the four tone contrasts of CVCV nouns; a pause group's nucleus (loudest stress, longest vowel) falls on the stressed syllable of the group's last word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; the only additional stress mentioned is on the first syllable of the former-verb-stem suffixes -k'ai, -hai, -koso (p. 8), which gives a word more than one stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: 'usually' stressed (hedged); the -kua suffix behaves irregularly for tone (p. 8); isolation-form phrase stress neutralizes noun tone contrasts (p. 3); intonation contours can override word tone (p. 4).
new_statements.identity_note: Gralow 1985 describes Coreguaje as spoken in Caquetá, Colombia (SIL fieldwork with mostly male consultants); no dialect distinctions are drawn. Cook & Levinsohn 1985 is the same variety.

Revista Brasileira de Linguística Antropológica 13: 347-366. doi:10.26512/rbla.v13i01.40360
tone_statements.quote: Igualmente, sobre esta línea se determina la estructura tonal de las palabras fonológicas, aspecto no tratado temáticamente en este trabajo ... En las representaciones fonéticas marcamos los tonos que hemos percibido a través del examen del corpus de datos obtenidos en nuestras grabaciones. De ninguna manera se trata de un estudio sistemático sino aproximativo. ... Las consonantes oclusivas sordas / p, t, k / se pronuncian como espiradas [ ph, th, kh ] cuando preceden a un núcleo silábico marcado con tono alto. ... a nivel suprasegmental existen dos aspectos compartidos predominantes: la nasalidad y la tonalidad.
tone_statements.translation: Likewise, on this [segmental] tier the tonal structure of phonological words is determined, an aspect not treated thematically in this work ... In the phonetic representations we mark the tones we have perceived through examination of the corpus of data obtained in our recordings. In no way is this a systematic study, only an approximate one. ... The voiceless stops /p, t, k/ are pronounced aspirated [ph, th, kh] when they precede a syllable nucleus marked with high tone. ... at the suprasegmental level there are two predominant shared features: nasality and tonality.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Koreguaje treated as tonal (high tone marked; H conditions aspiration of /p t k/ and glottal-stop insertion); no inventory given.

tone_statements.citation: Malaver Chaparro, Fabian Leonardo. 2021. Aproximación al sistema fonológico y morfofonológico de la lengua koreguaje (Amazonía noroccidental). Trabajo de grado (Lingüista), Departamento de Lingüística, Facultad de Ciencias Humanas, Universidad Nacional de Colombia, Bogotá. 119 pp.
tone_statements.quote: En la lengua parecen existir dos tonos contrastantes alto y bajo, aunque a nivel fonético es posible encontrar cinco tonos nivelados: extra alto, alto, medio, bajo y extra bajo; además de dos tonos modulados: descendente y ascendente. [...] Los tonos permiten diferenciar hasta 4 posibilidades de esquemas en bisílabos y hasta 7 posibilidades en trisílabos. [...] Fueron encontrados los siguientes pares mínimos tonales: (23). a. /tòá/ “Fuego” b. /tòà/ “Piernas” [...] Perdida de oposición o neutralización de A y B ante pausa o final absoluto: Ante final absoluto los tonos altos y bajos suelen realizarse como medios.
tone_statements.translation: The language appears to have two contrastive tones, high and low, although phonetically five level tones can be found: extra-high, high, mid, low and extra-low, plus two contour tones: falling and rising. [...] The tones distinguish up to 4 patterns on disyllables and up to 7 on trisyllables. [...] The following tonal minimal pairs were found: /tòá/ 'fire' vs /tòà/ 'legs' [...] Loss of opposition or neutralisation of H and L before pause or absolute final position: in absolute final position high and low tones are usually realised as mid.

tone_statements.quote: In the process of the analysis it finally became evident that stress was basically predictable, though tone was not. ... There are two tone levels in Coreguaje, high and low. (High tone is written ' and low tone is unmarked.) Words of two syllables contrast in all four possible sequences, e.g., high-high, hdma 'deer'; high-low, ndso 'monkeys'; low-high, rut^a 'flies'; and low-low, wekH 'tapirs'. ... An independent verb must have at least one high tone and one low tone. It cannot have more than three high tones.

sources.citation: Gralow, Frances L. (1985). The Coreguaje suprasegmental system: tone, stress and intonation. In Ruth M. Brend (ed.), From phonology to discourse: studies in six Colombian languages (SIL Language Data, Amerindian Series 9), 3-11. Dallas: SIL. [Glottolog 141826; printed title is 'Coreguaje: Tone, Stress, and Intonation']
sources.quote: In the process of the analysis it finally became evident that stress was basically predictable, though tone was not. [...] Every phonological word, sentence-level phrase, and sentence in Coreguaje has a tendency to fade away; that is, as a unit progresses, the syllables tend to become lower in pitch, shorter in length, and diminished in volume. The first syllable of a stem of a word is usually stressed. Stress is characterized by perceived loudness and length. [p. 8:] Two-syllable suffixes which have inherent high tone ... also seem to have stress on the first syllable as do stems.
sources.locator: p. 4 (end of §0 Introduction; §1 Stress and Rhythm); lines 50-51, 63-67; also p. 8 lines 531-533 and p. 8-9 §3(1) lines 561-563
sources.note: Stress is predictable (non-contrastive), realized by loudness and length, and falls on the first syllable of the stem ('usually'); two tones (H, L) are lexical on disyllabic stems; the pause-group nucleus (loudest stress, longest vowel) sits on the stressed syllable of the last word of the group; three historically stem-like bisyllabic suffixes (-k'ai benefactive, -hai accompanying movement, -koso probability) also carry stress on their first syllable, so a word can have more than one stressed syllable; in isolation 'phrase stress' neutralizes the tone contrasts of CVCV nouns (p. 3). This is…

sources.citation: Dupont Moreno, Carlos. 2021. La Estructura Sonora del Koreguaje: segmentos, supra-segmentos y proto-segmentos asociados a la armonía nasal en la lengua koreguaje (tukano occidental). Revista Brasileira de Linguística Antropológica 13: 347-366. doi:10.26512/rbla.v13i01.40360
sources.quote: Igualmente, sobre esta línea se determina la estructura tonal de las palabras fonológicas, aspecto no tratado temáticamente en este trabajo ... En las representaciones fonéticas marcamos los tonos que hemos percibido a través del examen del corpus de datos obtenidos en nuestras grabaciones. De ninguna manera se trata de un estudio sistemático sino aproximativo. ... Las consonantes oclusivas sordas / p, t, k / se pronuncian como espiradas [ ph, th, kh ] cuando preceden a un núcleo silábico marcado con tono alto. ... a nivel suprasegmental existen dos aspectos compartidos predominantes: la nasalidad y la tonalidad.
sources.note: Tone is not treated systematically; the author marks perceived tones (acute = tono alto) in phonetic transcriptions as an approximation (p. 356 and fn. 14); glottal stop generally appears before a high-toned syllable (fn. 18, p. 359); voiceless /p t k/ are aspirated before a syllable nucleus with high tone (fn. 20, p. 359); conclusion: nasality and tonality are the two predominant shared suprasegmental features of Tukanoan languages (p. 365). No tone inventory, nothing on stress/accent.

In the phonetic representations we mark the tones we have perceived through examination of the corpus of data obtained in our recordings. In no way is this a systematic study, only an approximate one. ... The voiceless stops /p, t, k/ are pronounced aspirated [ph, th, kh] when they precede a syllable nucleus marked with high tone. ... at the suprasegmental level there are two predominant shared features: nasality and tonality.

sources.quote: En la lengua parecen existir dos tonos contrastantes alto y bajo, aunque a nivel fonético es posible encontrar cinco tonos nivelados: extra alto, alto, medio, bajo y extra bajo; además de dos tonos modulados: descendente y ascendente. [...] Los tonos permiten diferenciar hasta 4 posibilidades de esquemas en bisílabos y hasta 7 posibilidades en trisílabos. [...] Fueron encontrados los siguientes pares mínimos tonales: (23). a. /tòá/ “Fuego” b. /tòà/ “Piernas” [...] Perdida de oposición o neutralización de A y B ante pausa o final absoluto: Ante final absoluto los tonos altos y bajos suelen realizarse como medios.
sources.note: Two contrastive tones (alto, bajo); phonetically five levels (extra-high to extra-low) and two contours (falling, rising); 4 tonal patterns on disyllables and 7 on trisyllables, tonal minimal pairs (/tòá/ 'fuego' vs /tòà/ 'piernas', /màã́/ 'camino' vs /máã́/ 'guacamaya'); tone processes: H/L neutralised to mid before pause, tonal dissimilation in diphthongs, fusion of identical H vowels into a long vowel with rising contour, H realised mid between L tones; §5.5.1: several suffixes (noun classifiers, some verbal suffixes) appear to lack fixed tone and take the tone opposite to the preceding sy…

tone.translation: The language appears to have two contrastive tones, high and low, although phonetically five level tones can be found: extra-high, high, mid, low and extra-low, plus two contour tones: falling and rising. [...] The tones distinguish up to 4 patterns on disyllables and up to 7 on trisyllables. [...] The following tonal minimal pairs were found: /tòá/ 'fire' vs /tòà/ 'legs' [...] Loss of opposition or neutralisation of H and L before pause or absolute final position: in absolute final position high and low tones are usually realised as mid.

sources.note: Its results as relayed by Rodríguez González 2000 (summarised in Malaver Chaparro 2021: 10-11): two contrastive tones (alto, bajo) and four tonological rules - tonal spreading within roots, tone alternation by tonal polarity from the end of the root, tonal lowering on the syllable after an elided low-tone vowel, tonal raising on the vowel before an elided high-tone syllable; aspirated stops analysed as allophones of plain stops before high tone.
